title: Curry Cruiser Second Revision
tagline: A structured Thai curry ordering flow for faster customers and cleaner food truck operations.
overview: Curry Cruiser is a Thai curry food truck concept that needs a digital ordering experience for predefined curry customization without free-text fields.
The UX challenge is dual-sided: customers need speed, confidence, and fallback access; staff need complete, kitchen-readable orders during rush service.

The recommended direction is a guided mobile curry builder with optional QR/direct entry, recommended combos, structured dietary handling, staff-ticket review, unavailable-option prevention, and clear confirmation.
problem: Food truck customers can hesitate or make ambiguous requests when customizing curry under time pressure, while staff lose time interpreting incomplete or unsupported orders.
solution: A mobile-first guided curry builder that captures required predefined choices, makes dietary constraints visible, supports non-QR fallback access, and turns the customer review into a staff-readable ticket.
role: UX research synthesis, product framing, design thinking artifacts, wireframe requirements
timeline: Concept pipeline through Stage 06 case study assembly
highlights: Separated customer ordering friction from staff operational friction.
Identified four provisional user groups: fast default seekers, careful choice makers, access-fragile customers, and rush-mode staff.
Converted the no-free-text constraint into structured dietary, unavailable, and unsupported-need handling.
Kept QR access optional because adoption signals are mixed.
Defined prototype-ready mobile screen requirements without enabling app build by default.

process.title: Research
process.summary: Desk research validated that off-premise ordering is common, speed and intuitive ordering matter, QR access has mixed customer reactions, and accessible mobile controls are non-negotiable.
insights: Fast off-premise ordering behavior is a credible context for Curry Cruiser.
QR should be treated as optional access rather than the value proposition.
No-free-text ordering needs structured exception handling.

process.title: Empathize
process.summary: Synthetic interviews produced provisional user groups and personas that clarify speed, dietary confidence, access resilience, and staff readability needs.
insights: Fast customers need defaults and short required choices.
Careful customizers need visible dietary and spice meaning.
Staff need tickets that require no interpretation.

process.title: Define
process.summary: The definition phase converted research and empathy patterns into testable problem statements and hypotheses.
insights: The ordering experience must solve both customer uncertainty and staff interpretation work.
Structured dietary choices are necessary to make no-free-text viable.
The staff ticket is a primary UX artifact.

process.title: Ideate
process.summary: The selected direction combines a guided curry builder, recommended combos, optional QR/direct entry, structured dietary handling, and a staff-ticket-style review.
insights: Recommended combos support speed without removing customization.
Disabled unavailable states prevent invalid orders.
Review screens should mirror staff fulfillment order.

userThreads.sourceInsight: Time-pressed customers value speed, defaults, and minimal required interaction when ordering food near the truck.

persona.name: Maya
persona.summary: A lunch customer near the truck with limited break time who wants a reliable curry without slowing the line.

userThreads.userStory: As a time-pressed lunch customer, I want a guided curry order with sensible defaults, so that I can submit confidently without slowing down the line.

journeySummary.scenario: Orders lunch near the truck during a short break.
journeySummary.keyPainPoint: Too many equal choices under time pressure.
journeySummary.opportunity: Recommended combo path with short required choices and a concise review.

userThreads.designImpact: Put recommended combos and required choices first, with optional customization secondary.

userThreads.sourceInsight: Customers with dietary, ingredient, or spice needs need visible confidence before they can trust a no-free-text ordering flow.

persona.name: Priya
persona.summary: A careful customizer who wants Thai curry but needs ingredient, dietary, and spice clarity before submitting.

userThreads.userStory: As a careful customizer, I want predefined dietary and spice choices that explain what they mean, so that I can order safely without typing special instructions.

journeySummary.scenario: Checks whether a curry order fits dietary and spice needs.
journeySummary.keyPainPoint: No visible way to represent restrictions without free text.
journeySummary.opportunity: Structured dietary controls, spice descriptions, and unsupported-need fallback.

userThreads.designImpact: Add structured dietary/allergen choices and keep those selections visible through review.

userThreads.sourceInsight: Staff need orders that are complete, standardized, and readable at a glance during peak service.

persona.name: Lina
persona.summary: A Curry Cruiser staff operator trying to keep orders accurate and moving during busy service.

userThreads.userStory: As a food truck staff member, I want every submitted order to arrive in a consistent kitchen-readable format, so that I can prepare it accurately during rush service.

journeySummary.scenario: Receives and prepares customized orders during rush.
journeySummary.opportunity: Required fields and staff-readable ticket sequence.

userThreads.designImpact: Make the customer review screen mirror the staff ticket structure.

keyDecisions.decision: Use a guided curry builder with required predefined choices.
keyDecisions.why: It reduces decision overload and prevents incomplete orders.
keyDecisions.impact: Customers get a faster path and staff receive complete tickets.

keyDecisions.why: QR ordering can help entry but can also create adoption, readability, privacy, or connectivity friction.
keyDecisions.impact: Customers can still order through direct links or staff fallback.

keyDecisions.decision: Represent dietary and allergy needs with structured choices.
keyDecisions.why: No-free-text ordering is only trustworthy if common constraints are visible and unsupported needs have a path.
keyDecisions.impact: Careful customers can decide whether the order is safe before submission.

keyDecisions.decision: Mirror the staff ticket in the review screen.
keyDecisions.why: The same structure helps customers check details and staff prepare orders accurately.
keyDecisions.impact: Reduces preventable clarification and fulfillment errors.

keyDecisions.decision: Defer payment, loyalty, delivery, and accounts.
keyDecisions.why: They add friction and are not validated as core to the current problem.
keyDecisions.impact: Keeps the prototype focused on ordering clarity and operational fit.

validation: Test whether users can complete a standard order in under two minutes.
Test whether users can identify whether a dietary restriction is supported before submit.
Test whether users can recover when QR scanning fails or is undesirable.
Test whether staff can interpret submitted orders without clarifying questions.
Test whether unavailable choices and unsupported needs prevent invalid orders.
outcome: The pipeline produced a research-backed concept and wireframe requirements for Curry Cruiser, with medium confidence because real customer and staff interviews are still needed.
nextSteps: Validate the exact curry option taxonomy against the real menu.
Prototype the guided builder and staff-ticket review.
Run usability tests for standard, dietary, QR fallback, and sold-out flows.
Decide whether payment belongs in scope after observing actual friction.
